meta.task_prompt:
Implement GitHub issue #9 on this repo: "add redis caching in auth proxy for kanban endpoints."

There is already a shared Redis client at `internal/pkg/redis/main.go`, and it is
already used elsewhere in the codebase (see `internal/app/server.go` and
`internal/pkg/server/permissions/perm.go` for the existing usage pattern). Follow
that same pattern rather than inventing a new one.

Scope:
- Add caching for the read paths in `internal/pkg/server/routes/kanban.go`.
- Add cache invalidation on the corresponding write paths, so a write never
  leaves a stale cached read behind.
- Pick sane key naming and TTLs consistent with how the existing Redis usage in
  this repo does it.
- This repo currently has no test files. Do not feel obligated to introduce a
  whole test framework for this change, but do double check the code compiles
  and, if there's an easy way to sanity-check the caching behavior manually
  (e.g. a local run), do that.

When you are done, close with a single clear paragraph summarizing exactly what
you changed and why — that summary becomes the pull request's title and body
verbatim, so make it read like a real PR description, not an internal note.

code_review.summary: The caching half of the PR is small and mostly copies the existing GetLabels/getItems pattern: read-through caching on GetLabel, getItem, exportKanban and getKanban, using the same 24h TTL, the X-cache: HIT header and the GetItemFromRedis/AddItemToRedis helpers. There are real problems, though. The three comment handlers now call DeleteAllKeysPrefix on an optional header. If that header is missing, the prefix is empty and the call flushes every key in Redis, including session keys. getItem builds its cache key from the client-supplied X-Board header, so the cached item is not tied to its real board, and a mismatched or missing header leaves stale reads for 24 hours. The getKanban cache wraps database.GetKanban, which always panics as written, so that path can never populate. More than half the diff is a repo-wide change that makes the storage, page and kanban RPC clients return pointers instead of values. It was done only to get a pre-existing `go vet` gate passing, it has nothing to do with issue #9, and it quietly changes error behavior: DeleteItem and DeleteComment now return 200 when the RPC fails. Finally, the PR title and body are the orchestrator's question to the user, not a PR description. No tests were added, and caching behavior was never exercised.

findings.summary: AddComment, UpdateComment and DeleteComment now call redis.DeleteAllKeysPrefix(c.Request.Header.Get("X-Board")). These handlers never otherwise need X-Board, so a request without it passes an empty prefix, and SCAN "*" deletes every key in Redis.
findings.failure_scenario: A client sends POST /kanban/comment?item_id=... with X-Auth and X-Session but no X-Board header. Header.Get returns "", so DeleteAllKeysPrefix("") scans the pattern "*" and deletes all keys, including every session (authId, sessionId, sessionId:authId). Every user is logged out and every cache is cleared. The same code is at lines 306 and 324.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard the invalidation: if boardId == "" skip it, or return 400. Better, add a guard inside DeleteAllKeysPrefix that refuses an empty prefix. That also protects the existing createItem/updateItem/DeleteItem callers.

findings.summary: The getItem cache key is `<X-Board header>:item:<id>`. The board comes from an optional client header, not from the item itself, so the key can drift from the board prefix that the write paths invalidate.
findings.failure_scenario: Client A calls GET /kanban/item?id=42 without X-Board, which caches under ":item:42". Or it sends a different board id than the one used on writes. A later PATCH /kanban/item with X-Board: B1 calls DeleteAllKeysPrefix("B1"), which never matches ":item:42". The next GET gets the stale item from cache for up to 24h.
findings.suggested_fix: Key the item cache on the item id alone (e.g. `item:<id>`) and delete that key explicitly in updateItem, DeleteItem and the three comment handlers, which already have the item or comment id. Otherwise, require X-Board (use Header["X-Board"][0] with a presence check, as the other handlers do) and skip caching when it is absent.

findings.summary: Switching `return *res` to `return res` changes failure behavior. Before, a nil gRPC response panicked inside the client, and gin.Recovery turned it into a 500. Now nil flows back to callers that ignore it and report success.
findings.failure_scenario: The kanban gRPC service is down during DELETE /kanban/item. The RPC error is only logged, DeleteItem returns a nil *VoidResp, the handler invalidates the cache and returns 200 "Item deleted" although nothing was deleted. DeleteComment behaves the same way (returns "OK"). In routes/page.go, CreateTemplate's result goes to c.JSON directly, so a failure now returns 200 `null` instead of 500.
findings.suggested_fix: Leave the RPC refactor out of this PR (see code-4). If it stays, return (res, err) from the client functions and have handlers answer 5xx on error, instead of relying on a nil-deref panic or silently succeeding.

findings.summary: Most of the diff (+50/-50 across internal/pkg/RPC/{kanban,page,storage}/main.go) is an unrelated signature change of every RPC client function from value to pointer. It was made only to clear pre-existing `go vet` copylocks errors.
findings.failure_scenario: Reviewers of a 'redis caching for kanban' PR get exported API changes in the page and storage packages, which nothing in issue #9 touches. That makes the PR harder to review and revert, and it hides the behavior change described in code-3.
findings.suggested_fix: Split it out: open a separate PR for the copylocks/pointer-return cleanup, with its own error-handling review. Keep this PR limited to routes/kanban.go and redis/main.go.

findings.summary: The new getKanban cache wraps database.GetKanban. That function does `if err := DB.Raw(...).Scan(&boardId); err != nil { panic(err) }`, and gorm's Scan returns a non-nil *gorm.DB, so it always panics. AddStringToRedis is never reached, and the cache path was never exercised.
findings.failure_scenario: GET /kanban always panics inside database.GetKanban, and gin.Recovery returns 500. The new cache is dead code, and nobody noticed because no request was ever run against it. The same function also concatenates the X-Useraccount header into raw SQL (a pre-existing SQL injection).
findings.suggested_fix: Fix GetKanban to check `.Error` and use a parameterized query (`DB.Raw("select board_id from user_accounts where id = ?", id)`), or at least note in the PR that this cache path is untested and that GetKanban is broken.

findings.summary: Board-wide invalidation uses a bare prefix with no separator (`<board>*`), so a write to board "abc" also clears the cache of any board whose id starts with "abc". The PR adds three more call sites of this pattern.
findings.failure_scenario: Board ids "12" and "123": a comment update on board 12 scans "12*" and deletes "123:export", "123:item:..." and so on. That is only needless cache churn, but it also means the prefix scan can match unrelated keys.
findings.suggested_fix: Invalidate with `boardId + ":"` as the prefix (all board-scoped keys already use `<board>:`), and reject an empty boardId.

findings.summary: No test and no manual run shows that any new cache path returns X-cache: HIT, or that any write actually invalidates. The only verification is that it compiles.
findings.failure_scenario: Bugs like code-1, code-2 and code-5 stay hidden because no request was ever made against a Redis-backed instance. The task explicitly asked for a local sanity check if easy.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a small miniredis-backed handler test for one read and write pair (e.g. getItem then updateItem), or document a manual curl sequence showing MISS, HIT, then MISS after a write.

findings.summary: The PR title and body are the orchestrator's interim message to the user. The title is "The reviewer stopped without completing (returned only a partial...", and the body asks "Would you like me to: 1. Try the review again...". It is not a PR description.
findings.failure_scenario: Anyone reading PR #16 sees internal engine chatter and a question addressed to someone else, not a summary of the change. The task required the closing paragraph to 'read like a real PR description'.
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite the title (e.g. "Add Redis caching and invalidation for kanban read endpoints") and replace the body with a real summary of the keys, TTL and invalidation points. If the vet refactor stays, list it separately.

process_review.summary: It started well. The ask agent ran a cheap-first survey (read_file, search, list_symbols) and produced a precise briefing, and the first coder (9d58fcf0) made targeted edits, always after reading the file, then ran `go build`. After that the run spent most of its budget working around a pre-existing `go vet` failure the task never asked about. The first coder stated it would 'build/vet' but ran only build, and it dismissed copylocks diagnostics that the diagnostics_triage judge rated high severity. The harness gate then failed and started a fix-up coder (10d09fde). That coder hit max_turns with zero edits: it ran an 87-second `find /` over the whole filesystem, dug through the Go module cache, masked vet's exit code with `| head`, and misread an empty file caused by a wrong redirect order as a clean result. The orchestrator then told the third coder that a 'partial copylocks fix already applied to storage/main.go' existed. It did not; no edits were made. It also turned the fix into a repo-wide RPC refactor, even though it had just told the user the failures were pre-existing and unrelated. The second reviewer repeated the same X-Board search three times, searched a vendor/ directory that does not exist, drew a loop_control repeating_itself score of 0.84, and stopped. The merge_gate record shows review_verdict: request_changes, yet the orchestrator told the user there was 'no verdict'. The run closed on a question to the user, and that question became the PR body. No manual sanity check of the caching was attempted. Six agents, 128 tool calls and about $1.98 for a roughly 50-line caching change is out of proportion. There were no read-before-edit violations.

findings.summary: The coder's stated intent was 'Now build/vet.', but it ran only `go build`. It never ran `go vet`, so it missed the gate the harness enforces.
findings.evidence: Line 89: reasoning "Now build/vet." and command "cd /workspace 2>/dev/null || cd .; go build ./... 2>&1 | head -100". No go vet call by this agent. The harness verify then failed on `go build ./... && go vet ./...` (transcript, reviewer 29f407f6 blocked).

findings.evidence: Line 76 response: "1:caused_by_this_edit": 0.84, "1:severity": {"score": 1.98, "confidence": 0.97}. Line 94 reasoning: "These warnings are pre-existing patterns ... not introduced by new logic issues ... No new errors."

findings.evidence: Line 139: `go vet ./... 2>&1 | head -100` shows exit code 0 with copylocks errors in the output. Line 143: exit code 1. Line 151: `go vet ./... 2>&1 > /tmp/vetout.txt; cat /tmp/vetout.txt`. Line 161: `cat /tmp/vetout.txt`, stdout (empty). This agent made no str_replace or apply_patch calls. The orchestrator's follow-up brief says a partial storage fix had already been applied, which is false. The previous coder made no edits, and the orchestrator didn't check the worktree before passing the claim on.

Lines 264-265: search path "vendor/..." gives "error: rg failed". Line 252: repeating_itself 0.74. Line 267: repeating_itself 0.84.

findings.summary: Compilation was checked: `go build` passed at lines 89 and 209, and `go vet` at line 212, though vet's exit code there came through `| head`. But no agent tried the manual caching sanity check the task asked for, and the run never said why it was skipped.
findings.evidence: Line 212: `go vet ./... 2>&1 | head -150`, exit code 0, empty output, which is the last verification run. No run_command anywhere in the trace starts the server, runs redis-cli, or issues curl requests. The task said: "if there's an easy way to sanity-check the caching behavior manually (e.g. a local run), do that."

findings.summary: The orchestrator's closing message was a status update plus a question to the user, not the required single-paragraph PR description, and it became the PR title and body verbatim.
findings.evidence: Transcript 01:27:07: "The reviewer stopped without completing ... Would you like me to: 1. Try the review again ... 2. Skip re-review and go straight to `settle_worktree`". pr.md title: "[reach-auth-proxy] The reviewer stopped without completing (returned only a partial".

findings.summary: Several judge calls failed or were truncated (loop_control at 87, 95 and 226; exec_approval at 137; truncated records at 179 and 181). The run carried on without that oversight and nothing reacted to the gaps.
findings.evidence: Lines 87, 95, 226: {"kind": "judge", "tag": "loop_control", "failed": true}. Line 137: exec_approval failed: true. Lines 179 and 181: {"kind": "judge", "truncated": true, "original_chars": 17564/17245}.

findings.summary: Although it continued from 10d09fde, the third coder re-read almost every file the previous agent had read. That included the first 200 lines of auth.go, when a targeted search at line 207 was enough to show auth.go doesn't call these RPCs.
findings.evidence: Lines 169-177 re-read storage/page/kanban main.go; lines 192/194 kanban.go; lines 199/201 page.go; line 204 storage.go; line 206 auth.go lines 1-200; line 207 search in auth.go gives "(no matches)".

strengths: The ask agent's survey was thorough and cheap-first. It correctly found GetLabels/getItems as the real reference pattern and flagged that getKanban returns a raw string.
The caching edits follow the existing repo idiom: the same helpers, the 24h TTL, the X-cache: HIT header and `<board>:` key naming.
No read-before-edit violations. Every str_replace and apply_patch came after a read_file of the same path.
`go build ./...` and `go vet ./...` were verified with real exit codes in the trace (lines 89, 209, 212).
concerns: Comment handlers can flush all of Redis, sessions included, when X-Board is absent (code-1).
The item cache key depends on an optional client header, so writes may not invalidate it (code-2).
An unrelated repo-wide RPC pointer refactor is bundled in and turns some RPC failures into 200 responses (code-3, code-4).
The getKanban cache is dead code on top of a GetKanban function that always panics, and no caching behavior was ever exercised (code-5, code-7).
The PR title and body are an internal question to the user, not a description (code-8, process-11).

The fix-up coder burned max_turns with zero edits, the orchestrator passed on a false claim that a fix had been applied, and the reviewer stopped with request_changes that was reported as 'no verdict'.
overall_assessment.narrative: The core caching change is reasonable in shape, but the invalidation strategy has a dangerous empty-prefix case and a header-dependent key that can go stale, so it isn't safe to merge as is. The process went wrong once the first coder skipped `go vet`. That triggered a harness failure the run handled poorly: an unproductive fix-up agent, a false state claim, and scope creep into unrelated packages. The run then ended with a stopped reviewer and a question to the user posted as the PR body. The feature work needs a focused revision, and the vet cleanup should go into its own PR.
